loop.text: A data analyst interview usually comes in three parts. First, a SQL screen, live or as a take-home. A few questions on spreadsheets and statistics. And a conversation that starts with: how would you analyze this?

probe.text: Across the three parts, interviewers probe four things. SQL fluency: joins, GROUP BY, WHERE against HAVING, CASE, and window functions. Framing: picking the right grain, meaning what one row stands for, handling nulls, and not counting anything twice after a join. Communication: your assumptions, your caveats, and what you'd check next. And tools: a spreadsheet, and a BI tool, short for business intelligence, like Tableau, Power BI or Looker.

ai.text: AI, artificial intelligence, has changed some of it. Checking now matters more than writing, because a plausible query is cheap to produce. Expect to be handed one an assistant wrote, and asked: is it right?

series.text: This series follows the track, one video per topic page, from SQL to AI-assisted analysis: a hundred and fifty-six questions in all, each answered once, in the video of the page it belongs to.

practice.text: And every page has concept checks of its own, four of them add runnable challenges, and a bank of a hundred and ten multiple-choice questions covers the whole track.

next.text: Almost every interview has a SQL screen, so the series starts there. Next: SQL.

series-how.text: Each video works through the questions that need a figure, then takes the rest quickly.

ai-use.text: You'll be asked how you use these tools responsibly: what you'd paste into one, how you disclose using it, and how you keep hallucinated insights out of a report.

ai-bi.text: BI tools now answer questions asked in plain language, but they only answer correctly on top of clean, well-defined metrics, and providing those is becoming the analyst's job.

ai-off.text: And the live SQL round is usually AI-off, so fluency still matters. Ask the recruiter about each round.
